content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a framework for studying biases of large pretrained models for code generation. The framework entails manipulating the prompt consisting of three main components: function name, NL description, and examples. They propose three different methods for this manipulation: anonymizing the function name to “func”, removing one/all keywords from the NL description, and removing all examples. On three different datasets, they show that performance degrades when the prompts are manipulated in this way. In additional experiments, they study whether augmenting the training set with such adversarial examples can improve performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The motivation for studying biases for large pretrained models for code generation is nice and very important given the way the field is progressing. 
- The idea to analyze different aspects of the prompt as a way of studying bias is also nice and has the potential to shed light into how prompts should be designed in the future for this task.
- Extensive empirical evaluation across many different models.

Weaknesses:
- It seems to me that the framework is not well-grounded with realistic data manipulations. In Section 1, it is written “Suggested changes resemble typical errors of a human coder.” However, it is not clear whether the three types of changes introduced in this work do in fact resemble typical errors of a human coder. For example, how likely is it for a human coder to use the generic “func” method name rather than a more descriptive name? Or how likely it is for a human coder to write an NL description without any keywords?
- In general, the manipulations that are done should be semantically-preserving, and it is not clear whether the three techniques used in this work have that property. Namely, removing keywords from the description can render the description meaningless or even drastically change its meaning. Changing a descriptive method name to “func” is also not semantically-preserving. Although the authors are expecting the model to deduct the missing context from the other blocks, it is not clear whether all blocks are going to be comprehensive in the data. For example, in Figure 1, what if the “list” keyword was only in the description? Removing this keyword from the description and deducing this concept from a method name titled rev_take2 and example rev_take2([a,2,apple]) would be more difficult.
- The authors repeatedly claim that any failure that happens when the method name is replaced with “func” is an indication that the model has memorized the training data/”copied-pasted” from the training data. However, there is no empirical evidence that is presented to support this claim. Couldn’t it be that the method name contained information that was not present in the other two blocks? Or that the “func” keyword is associated with certain things in the training data that is causing confusion at test time?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity
- In Section 4, a subsection is titled “Finetuning and evaluation.” However, it says “the experiments are done in a zero-shot fashion for all datasets and models.” It is not clear whether finetuning was done.
- In 6.2, details about the training data augmentation and finetuning are not clear. Namely, how many examples were added. Was it task-specific finetuning or the same pretraining objective? If it was task-specific finetuning, then there is a missing experiment on how the model performs with just the finetuning and no data augmentation.
- It is not clear why the “Before” columns of Table 5 don’t line up with the Codeparrot numbers presented in Table 8. Also, some of the numbers between “Before” and “After” are very close in Table 5. Was statistical significance measured?

Quality
I find there to be some fundamental issues with the underlying framework in this work that make me question the overall quality of this work.

Novelty
There has been some work which studies the generalizability of code generation models (e.g., https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.03758.pdf) as well as adversarial training for code generation models. However, to the best of my knowledge, there is no work that does fine-grained analysis of the prompt for large code generation models as done in this work. Therefore, I find the motivation behind this work to be novel and interesting. Additionally, while there have been a number of papers which propose ways for acquiring semantically-preserving code transformations for data augmentation, there has been no work on how to do this for the input that goes into code generation models. Although the execution of this is weak in my opinion, the idea is relatively novel.


Reproducibility
While the authors use publicly available models and datasets, their adversarial data would need to be released to reproduce the results.
content.summary_of_the_review: While I appreciate the motivation in trying to identify biases in the prompts for large pretrained models for code generation, I find the overall execution to be weak and not well-grounded. The techniques used to manipulate the data for identifying these biases are not necessarily realistic or semantics-preserving. It seems that the available context is being substantially reduced/altered, and the authors are attributing the resulting performance degradation to bias, which may not be the case.

content.title: Response to reviewers comments
content.comment:
We are happy that the reviewer shares our thoughts regarding the novelty of searching for biases in the code domain. We have updated our work and would like to comment on the reviewer's points. 


**Regarding the first point: It seems to me that the framework is..:**

In our work, we introduce the following primary sources of possible errors:
* Anonymization: The case of an uninformative function name instead of a more descriptive one
* Keyword Drop: The case of a missing keyword from the problem description - given that its context can be deducted from the remaining code.
* Example Drop: The removal of example cases in the description which act as demonstrations of the function's operation

In the first case, we conducted the following experiment: We used KeyBert to measure the embedding similarity between each detected function name and words in its comments/description. As a match, we count every case where there is at least one word with over 0.8 cosine similarity. We took a sample of 20.000 python files and found that for slightly less than 8%, such matches do not exist. In non-matching instances, function names do not correspond to any comments or context in the docstring, acting as a mere placeholder similar to the “func” keyword we introduce. Additionally, we have included two new experiments. In Appendix A.8, we show that function names highly correlated to the task can be misleading if taken as the sole source of information. In Appendix A.9, we present cases where names are the root of highly biased completions. 

In the case of keywords, previous studies [1,2] present that in the case of student programmers, the most common non-syntax mistakes consist of using wrong keywords as variables/function names and mismatched types or arguments in methods/definitions. Additionally, studies involving code reviews [3,4] found that the most popular issues that programmers failed to correct were poorly descriptive documentation, misleading comments, and naming conventions that impacted the reusability of their code.
 In our work, identified keywords derive from such sources. Due to our semantic-preservation steps, the chosen keywords to be removed correspond to duplicate or easily deductible arguments, types, or variables from the rest of the function body. This holds true both in the case of one or multiple keywords being dropped at the same time. Identified keywords are highly correlated with the error-prone function sections, which, as discussed, can be deeply uninformative or simply non-existent. 


Finally, regarding the removal of examples, a search in the web-scraped open-source dataset of CodeParrot reveals that docstring examples are scarce (<1%). On the contrary, examples in docstrings are far more common (almost always existent) in datasets that come from competition challenges. In [5], the authors compare model performance in few-shot scenarios, where correct, buggy or no additional examples were added to the context. Inspired by this, we decided to test the equivalent phenomenon on docstring examples and, consequently, the effect that a coding habit, such as adding documentation examples, could have on model performance and bias reliance.

[1] Investigating novice programming mistakes: educator beliefs vs. student data, Brown et al. ICER 2014.

[2] Open-Source Software in Class: Students' Common Mistakes, Hu et al. ICSE-SEET 2018.

[3] Modern Code Reviews in Open-Source Projects: Which Problems Do They Fix? Beller et al.MSR 2014

[4] Assessing the Students' Understanding and their Mistakes in Code Review Checklists, CY Chong, et al. ICSE'21-JSEET 2021

[5] Evaluating Large Models Trained on Code, Chen et al. https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374v2 2021

content.title: Response to reviewers comments - Part 2
content.comment:
**Regarding the maintenance of semantic information:**

Parts of our method are specifically designed for this cause. We use a combination of semantic similarity search and ruled-based filtering to avoid removing critical information.  

Therefore, even though we might destroy local semantics, the global semantics is still preserved and sufficient to solve the task. We guarantee that our keyword identification mechanism works correctly: Each time a model gives a wrong prediction under the effect of an anonymized function, we always make sure that relevant keywords exist both in the description and/or the examples given.
We remove duplicate or redundant information that can be collected from different parts of the function name, description, or examples.

We ensure that any omitted parts can be found or deducted from the remaining context of the problem. In this way, we challenge the reasoning abilities of the model under test rather than simply making the problem more dubious.

Furthermore, we adopt a test introduced in [1,2] to quantify the degree that semantics are preserved in our method. This test estimates how differently a language model understands the same text before and after perturbations. 

Since it was applied in natural language and coding scenarios, we found it appropriate for our work. We have updated our work and added the above tests in Section 5.3. Our results show that even in the harshest of our methods (Anonymize + Drop All), the models assign around 95% similarity between the coding challenge before and after changes.

**Regarding: _However, no empirical evidence is presented to support this claim_**

We decided to test our hypothesis of models heavily relying on function names and resorting to copying behaviors. For this reason, we used the open-source CodeParrot dataset to look for “copying” behavior during code generation.
In Appendix Section A.9, we present some incorrect completions generated by CodeParrot(1.5B) and the "heavily inspired" files where the responses were found. Furthermore, we show that in the case of anonymization, responses differ, with the description of the problem staying intact.

**Regarding: _Couldn’t it be that the method name contained information not present in the other two blocks?_**

Each coding challenge is always accompanied by an analytic description and examples.  Most function names describe, at best, the general spirit of the task and give almost zero directions to its solution. There are no examples of challenges where the function name is more than an already existing hint in the description or cannot be easily deducted from the examples. For example, in HumanEval, there exist tasks where the function name is closely related to the task but misleading if it was to be taken as the only source of information. We provide our intuitions and completions from Codex-v2 when asked to generate a function based only on its name. 
We observe that the function name is hinting the model in another direction. We propose that function names can reinforce the model towards a correct generation but under no circumstances are sufficient. We present more examples in Appendix A.8

**Regarding: _Or that the “func” keyword is associated with certain things in the training data that are causing confusion at test time?_**

No, func is just a random keyword that, in the open-sourced Codeparrot dataset, is not once used as a self-contained function name accompanied by any prompt. We repeated the same experiment with other keywords, such as action, do_stuff, or a plain xyz, and we get the same results.


[1] Break-It-Fix-It: Unsupervised Learning for Program Repair Yasunaga et al. ICML 2021

[2] LM-Critic: Language Models for Unsupervised Grammatical Error Correction Yasunaga et al. EMNLP 2021

content.title: Response to reviewers comments - Part 3
content.comment:
**On Clarity comment 1:**
The section name has been corrected. We analyze experimental-specific details and do not refer to the finetuning experiments of section 6.2 yet.

**On Clarity comment 2:**
During the fine-tuning experiments in section 6.2, we use the whole of the MBPP and DMCC datasets, with each coding instance replicated for each available augmentation.

Thus, both dataset sizes are multiplied by seven, with each augmentation involving the “drop one” method being applied randomly to any - if available - keywords to be dropped. This results in roughly 64,000 problems. 
The fine-tuning objective is still a next-token prediction, except that models are conditioned initially on the modified prompt instead of a “start of sentence” token. 
In this way, we focus our learning objective on creating correct solutions based on a challenging prompt rather than modeling term co-occurrence in the prompt itself. 
We have also conducted the same experiment by simply fine-tuning non-augmented examples of the MBPP and DMCC datasets. In this experiment, models exhibited no improvements against any perturbations. You can find this study in Appendix Section A7.

**On Clarity comment 3:**
The cause of misalignment between Tables 5 and 8 was that we initially presented the results of a single fixed seed in Tables 5 / 6. Both Tables have been updated to averages of 15 runs. We have also conducted a T-Test between the samples of each perturbation method before and after fine-tuning. We use bold to signify a significant increase in performance with at least 95% confidence (a = 0.05).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper explores the biases in a LLM's coding ability by procedurally removing various kinds of information from the prompt (such as function names, examples, and keywords). The paper evaluates several different models such as Codex, InCoder, and Bloom and on multiple different public datasets such as HumanEval, MBPP, and Deep Mind's Code contests dataset and shows that all of these models have the above mentioned biases. The paper also used their prompt transformation technique to create additional data to allow for robust finetuning of some of the above models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**

- Understanding the biases of large language models is an important research topic and as far as I know, they are no such studies specifically for code domains. 

- The results in the paper showcasing the various biases in the models are interesting to read (although they are a bit expected).

**Weaknesses:**

- The paper would have been stronger if it can draw some insights into how the pretraining strategy (dataset or architecture or training objectives) impacted the biases in the different models.  

- The adversarial training part proposed in the paper is for finetuning the models rather than pretraining. It is not clear how the proposed technique would scale to pretraining dataset especially because the dataset is not very well formatted. 

- The results in Section 6.2 (adversarial finetuning part) don't look like significant improvements. These might also mean that it is very important to handle adversarial training during pre-training rather than during finetuning.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is novel and mostly well written except for the following additional points: 

- The transformation algorithms for the name blocks and the example blocks seem straightforward to me, but the keyword filtering part seems very adhoc. From the description in section 5.2, it is not clear to me if the keyword filtering algorithm is doing what it is supposed to do. For example, in Figure 2, why is "shortest" in the filtered keywords? It is not in either the name block or the example block, so shouldn't it be discarded? More detailed rules and examples might help. 

- Tables 5 and 6 should include a baseline that does regular finetuning on the datasets (without the data augmentation). This is a very important baseline to measure the impact of data-augmentation.

- The paper mentions that the models might be memoizing based on the function name. One interesting experiment to test this hypothesis is to directly measure the amount of copying for  models such as CodeParrot whose pretraining dataset is publicly available.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper tackles an important problem of finding biases in code LLM's. The paper is mostly well-writing and the bias results are very interesting. However, the second part of the paper that explores adversarial training is only restricted to finetuning stages (rather than pretraining) and the results are not very significant here (and is missing an important baseline).

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a mechanism to test "biases" in code generation models. The authors propose three transformations to the input that would not affect a human's comprehension of the input. They further show that the performance of certain code generation models drop when these transformations are applied to their input, thus implying that there is a misalignment between a human's and a model's comprehension of the input.

They then use this insight to fine-tune the models on adversarially transformed inputs, and show that the models become more resilient to the same transformations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths :**

1. Generalizable, model-agnostic framework.

1. The transformations (for the most part) are such that a human's comprehension of the code would not be affected.

1. Clear drops in performance across models, and clear improvement in robust performance because of adversarial training.

**Weaknesses :**

**Point 1:**

I have a major issue with the following statement, which forms the basis for the "Anonymize" transform and the assumptions thereof.  

*"...any inability of the model to generate a correct solution can be attributed to cues related to the function name itself; indicating that the tested model “copied-pasted” a solution from training data and it has not learned how to program."*

Especially in the case of descriptive function names like `add_two_nums`, this is as good as the problem description! A human given the function header `add_two_nums(a, b)` would be perfectly capable of coming up with `return a+b`. Renaming it to `func` destroys useful *semantic* information that the model could use, and does not just disrupt its memorization. In my opinion, a better test would be to rename it to something that is semantically equivalent but not identical. For example, `add_numbers` or `add_two_ints`.

Another way to make this work would be to consider only those functions whose names have no semantic meaning (like `func`, `foo`, etc). Then does changing *those* names lead to a drop in performance? That would be clear memorization bias.

I can appreciate that in the case of more sophisticated problems, it may be impossible to get the entire description from the function name. But the function name is still useful semantic information that is being removed! So it is only natural to see a drop in performance. I disagree with the "memorization" conclusion.

**Point 2 :**
I do feel that the key insight is not surprising. Deep learning models use multiple streams of data to make their decision, and depriving the model of any one stream of information is bound to lead to some degradation of performance. To make a computer vision analogy, this would be the equivalent of masking key portions of an image and seeing how that affects classification accuracy.

If the authors could conclusively demonstrate some kind of "memorization" bias (see Point 1), then that would be interesting and unexpected.

The robustness fine-tuning experiments also have unsurprising results : tuning a model on adversarial examples is bound to improve performance on the same types of examples. For actionable feedback, see Point 3.

**Point 3 :**

How does the *natural* performance of the model change after the robustness training? That is, how does the model perform on code examples without any transformations? Often, training with adversarial examples has an adverse effect on natural accuracy. In this case, one can interpret the adversarial training as trying to "spread" the model's attention over all parts of the input as opposed to relying on one part. Does this improve the model's overall performance? That would be interesting.

This should definitely be a point of comparison in Table 5 and Table 6, with a "Before" and "After" comparison too.

**Point 4 (minor suggestion) :**

This sort of study would be strengthened with some visualization of attention weights or gradient maps. If the model is truly generating code by "memorizing" the function name, then we would expect large attention weights on the function name and low weights everywhere else. Similarly for the other cases involving keyword deletion, etc.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity :**

In my opinion, a couple of aspects of the presentation of the paper could be improved :

1. In Figure 2, it looks like both the Name Block and the Description Block are being fed to KeyBert, which threw me off for a while. Would be nice if that arrow could be shifted down a bit.

1. What are the bold elements in Table 3, 4, 5, 6? This should be explained in the captions.

**Quality and Novelty :**

I like the attempt to systematically expose flaws, but I do feel that the paper falls short of that goal. It is not clear to me that the drop in performance is unreasonable or unexpected for the transformations performed.

**Reproducibility :**

I could not see code shared by the authors to reproduce their results, but their algorithm description is thorough enough that I think it would be possible to reproduce the results from scratch with some effort.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper attempts to expose biases in deep learning models. However I find the conclusions unsurprising and/or not completely founded, and I feel that further experiments could improve the paper. I have provided actionable feedback to address my concerns under the "Weaknesses" section.

content.title: Response to reviewers comments
content.comment:
We want to thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestions. Figure 2 was indeed confusing and is now redesigned. A clear description accompanies all tables. We want to address the reviewer's comments.

**Regarding Point 1:**

On the maintenance of semantic information, parts of our method are specifically designed for this cause. We use a combination of semantic similarity search and ruled-based filtering to avoid removing critical information.

In the case of the "add_two_nums" example, just as with every problem in our analysis, we state that the problem comes with a task description. In this case, even when swapping the function name with a generic token, the model can still read the problem description such as:     “Generate a function that adds two numbers and returns their sum." Therefore, even though we might change local semantics, the global semantics is still preserved and is sufficient to solve the task. We guarantee that our keyword identification mechanism works correctly: Each time a model gives a wrong prediction under the effect of an anonymized function, we always make sure that relevant keywords exist both in the description and/or the examples given.

Our experiments reveal that models prefer specific keyword choices and even the location of those keywords in the problem formulation. If a code generation model solely relies on the "add_two_nums" function name, completely disregarding the problem description, doesn't it heavily suffer from bias? By exploring the open-source CodeParrot dataset, we have found instances where the function name itself heavily guides the model to whole or partial solutions copied from training examples. Anonymization of the same function leads to different generations. You can find this newly added experiment in Appendix Section A.9


As the reviewer correctly mentions, a human can complete the code snippet without looking at the description. Nevertheless, this is not the case in any of our methods. 
The problem description is always present. We remove duplicate or redundant information that can be collected from different parts of the function name, description, or examples. We ensure that any omitted parts can be found or deducted from the remaining context of the problem. In this way, we challenge the reasoning abilities of the model under test rather than simply making the problem more dubious. 

Furthermore, we adopt a test introduced in [1,2] to quantify the degree that semantics are preserved in our method. This test estimates how differently a language model “understands” the same text before and after perturbations. Since it was applied in natural language and coding scenarios, we found it appropriate for our work.

We collect a random sample of 200 coding challenges from the HumanEval and MBPP. Each challenge is then modified according to each of our proposed methods. Then for the original and every modified version of a challenge, we calculate their log probability score using a large language model trained on code. The main idea in [1,2] is that the model will act as a soft critic, ranking modified prompts by their overall comprehensibility. Poorly understood modified prompts will be assigned a log probability score far lower than the unmodified one. We calculate log probability similarity as: $ 100 - \frac{LogProbMethod - LogProbOriginal}{LogProbOriginal} $

Our results show that even in the harshest of our methods (Anonymize + Drop All), our model critic (Codex-v2) assigns around 95% similarity between the coding challenge before and after changes. Modified challenges introduce little confusion to models under test.  We have updated our work and added the above tests in Section 5.3.

content.title: Response to the authors
content.comment:
I appreciate the authors' changes to address review comments. It is good to see that adversarial training does not negatively affect performance on the original data.

However, I still do not feel comfortable increasing my score for the following reasons:

1. This paper is essentially about robustness against certain transformations. It is my opinion that this is *not* "bias" as per the usual definition. In the next revision, I would recommend avoiding the term completely.

1. I am still not convinced that "memorization bias" actually has anything to do with *memorization*.

   > Our experiments reveal that models prefer specific keyword choices and even the location of those keywords in the problem formulation. If a code generation model solely relies on the "add_two_nums" function name, completely disregarding the problem description, doesn't it heavily suffer from bias? By exploring the open-source CodeParrot dataset, we have found instances where the function name itself heavily guides the model to whole or partial solutions copied from training examples. Anonymization of the same function leads to different generations.

   I agree that this indicates that the model relies heavily on the function name, and that is useful to know. But this does not mean that it has *memorized* the function name from the training dataset. It could be using semantic information in the function name.

1. Adversarial robustness is usually studied against transformations that leave a human's comprehension of the input almost unaffected, but result in large significant drops in model performance. In this case, I am not convinced that the drops in performance are larger than would be expected for the transformations applied. Example - if I randomly masked out portions of an image or added Gaussian noise, and the performance of an image classifier fell from 95% to 85%, that would be a drop in performance, but not unexpected. This is just measuring performance against a domain shift (not an *adversarial* domain shift).

1. *Regarding the similarity entropy measure:* I like the attempt to define a semantic similarity metric, but I am not sure this definition is watertight. It is possible for two sentences to both be very probable according to a language model, in which case their similarity according to this definition will be 100%. But that does not necessarily mean that the sentences are similar to each other! Sentence 1 and Sentence 2 may just be very grammatical sentences, eg, "I have a dog", "It is raining", but they have nothing to do with each other.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies the robustness of large language models trained on source code. Specifically, the paper proposed a framework to identify if a code language model is sensitive toward information such as keywords in function docstrings, function names, function arguments, and sample test cases that may present in function docstrings. Hand-crafted rules (such as verbs carrying key information) and model training approaches are explored to identify key information that large code models are sensitive to. Then experiments are conducted in different settings, e.g., drop one or all identified keywords, drop test case examples in the docstring, and function name replaced by an arbitrary token. Experiment results show that existing models are sensitive to such information, and when they are not present, these models fail to achieve the same performance. As a remedy, this work augmented code data and finetuned models to show improvements in code completion tasks. Thus, models become more robust.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
__Strength__
- The paper is overall nicely written. Apart from a few grammar and punctuation issues, the paper is clear.
- Clear description of experiment setup and comprehensive experiments.
- Given the rapid progress of code language models in recent times, the main topic of the paper is timely and useful.

__Weakness__
- There are several weaknesses. First of all, the paper mixed bias and robustness concepts. Though I understood what authors wanted to refer to in places, I find it bad to mix them up. I am particularly noting this because bias and robustness are two very widely studied issues in the literature. Therefore, to accurately position this paper in the literature, writing should be improved.
- As a follow-up to the last point, the paper misses the discussion of relevant robustness works in the related works. I found the two paragraphs, "Bias in large language models" and "Probing reasoning through biases" irrelevant to this work.
- While the paper discusses irrelevant works, the paper misses out on discussing many relevant works in software engineering. There are papers that studied the impact of identifier naming on tasks such as code summarization. However, they are overlooked.
- The second big issue I see in this work is the bad choice of experiment models. Codeparrot is merely an example of a code completion model (sort of toy model); it is not a well-trained model (if we look at its performance, it will be clear). On the other hand, Incoder is primarily designed for code insertion tasks, and Bloom is not a code language model. Therefore, it is hard to accept the conclusions derived from experiments in this work. CodeGen (CodeGen: An Open Large Language Model for Code with Multi-Turn Program Synthesis) is perhaps a better model for this study, given that the model is available in 4 different sizes.
- Finally, the third weakness of this work is the significance of the scientific contribution of this work. I find it really thin that it cannot pass the bar of a top ML conference like ICLR.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
__Clarify and Quality__
Overall, the paper is clear and easily understandable. However, more discussion and acknowledgment of related works are needed.

__Novelty__
The significance of this work is very narrow.

__Reproducibility__
I can gauge the effort behind this work. Unless the code is released, it will be hard to reproduce the results of this work. Therefore, I encourage the authors to release the source code whenever the paper is published.
content.summary_of_the_review: Due to a lack of discussion of the relevant literature, strong evaluation, and scientific contribution, I vote to reject this work.

content.title: Response to reviewers comments
content.comment:
We are glad that the reviewer shares our points on the importance of code language model research. We want to address the points mentioned in the review.

**Regarding the first three points:**

Our work positions between biases in large language models (LLMs) or code generation models that are based on LLMs, and robustness in reasoning-based generational processes. This is not the typical setting of robustness in machine learning, where attacks might not be attributed to biases like per-pixel perturbations[1,2,3,4]. Our attacks are more closely related to “semantic perturbations” where semantically meaningful units are changed. E.g., attacks could change lighting conditions or genders in tasks where these changes should be irrelevant. Here, poor performance of models could be attributed (but not limited) to various biases that exist in datasets. We also adapted a standard strategy to robustify models against these attacks (Section 6.2 Tables 5 and 6), which includes the perturbed dataset in the training set for fine-tuning. However, we would be grateful if the reviewer could point out specific works that we miss and clarify what the reviewer meant by “mixing biases and robustness”.

Furthermore, our primary motivation came from studies of LLMs bias induced by the introduction/removal of specific words/sentence structures. With the rising research interests in code generation models that are based on LLMs, we investigate if such effects carry on to these models due to their LLM core mechanism. Since that, we cite works related to LLMs, and biases in LLMs or reasoning models.

Generating code is not limited to understanding the language description of the task at hand but also performing algorithmic reasoning to create a solution.We illustrate such cases of reasoning failures in Section 7, Figures a-d.

**Regarding the fourth point:**

We test not only Codeparrot but also stronger models (Section 4, Table 2) for code generation. Codeparrot is a valuable inclusion to our experiment since it comes with an open-source dataset and is easily used for further finetuning experiments. Especially its smaller variant (110M) achieves competitive results to other open-source LLMs (PolyCoder, GPT-Neo) at even larger parameter sizes. Furthermore, by exploring CodeParrot’s dataset we validated our hypothesis of function names acting as biases to code generation. Models can be heavily inspired by similarly named examples in their training set and resort to copying whole or parts of the solution instead of actually performing reasoning. You can find this experiment in Appendix Section A.9

We chose InCoder because it was trained under a novel bidirectional objective, despite being a generative model. Our initial thought was that our methods would not have such a strong effect on it since it has enhanced context understanding capabilities. Tables 3 and 4 show that our methods are just as effective on this model.

Quoting directly from Comparison to Left-to-Right Generative Models on Code Synthesis 6.1 of the InCoder Paper(https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.05999.pdf):

*We note that our model achieves roughly comparable performance on the HumanEval metrics to CodeGen-Multi [46], which is also a ∼6B parameter model trained on roughly the same amount of Python code, as well as AlphaCode’s 1.1B decoder-only model [44] which also uses a similar amount of Python training data.*

For the sake of completeness, we applied our methods to two variants of the CodeGen(Mono) Model, as suggested by the reviewer, which can be found in Tables 3 and 8. We observe a similar pattern of performance degradation as with any other model tested.

Finally, the Bloom model exhibits emergent abilities in multiple domains by training on massive multilingual and multi-purpose content. Despite not being a code generation model, it performs equally well with code-specific models in the same parameter budget. This could mean that techniques such as dropping keywords or anonymization should be less effective since Bloom's strong point is language understanding. The exact opposite argument could be made for the "drop examples" method . A model like Bloom would benefit from these demonstrations just as other Massive scale LLMs did in recent studies (GPT3, Megatron-LM etc).
Also such a model might be challenging for us since bias effects can theoretically be reduced when a model is exposed to diverse training examples. In our experiments, however, we reveal that this is still not the case under our setup, and post-training solutions are thus explored.


[1] Feature Denoising for Improving Adversarial Robustness, Xie et al. CVPR 2019

[2] Disentangling Adversarial Robustness and Generalization Stutz et al. CVPR 2019

[3] Are Transformers More Robust Than CNNs? Bai et al. NeurIPS 2021

[4] ME-Net: Towards Effective Adversarial Robustness with Matrix Estimation ICML 2019
